topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; competency frameworks may have limited direct application to Australian organisational settings or non-healthcare sectors, though core AI literacy principles may transfer.
takeaways: Digital health competency frameworks in Europe emphasise domain-specific skills alongside AI literacy — consider how your AI development program balances technical capabilities with sector-contextual knowledge relevant to your employees' roles.

Scoping reviews of competency frameworks typically identify gaps between current workforce capabilities and future needs; use this as a model to audit what AI literacy gaps exist in your own organisation before designing targeted interventions.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on public health education contexts and faculty development. Generalisability to other sectors or non-academic settings unclear without access to full methodology.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption is addressable through structured development programs; design these to move educators from scepticism to confidence rather than assuming buy-in.
AI literacy initiatives in health education should target teaching staff first — their readiness directly influences whether students gain practical AI competency.
Use faculty development as a lever for institutional change: training educators to teach AI competently can shift organisational culture faster than top-down mandates.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development requires adaptation. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet.
takeaways: AI literacy for non-specialists should be embedded within broader digital literacy frameworks rather than taught in isolation, helping learners understand AI's role alongside other digital tools and competencies.

A 'holistic' approach suggests integrating AI concepts across multiple competency domains (e.g., critical thinking, data interpretation, ethical reasoning) — consider similar cross-functional integration when designing AI upskilling for diverse employee groups.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited by lack of detail in snippet — appears to focus on higher education contexts, which may not directly transfer to workplace AI capability development for employees in organisations.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most critical for your organisation's roles, as educational strategies may need adaptation for adult learners with existing domain expertise.
Consider how higher education's pedagogical approaches to AI literacy (e.g. project-based learning, interdisciplinary teams) could be customised for employee training programs.

Recognise that developing AI competencies requires more than technical skills — review how the article addresses foundational knowledge, critical thinking, and ethical reasoning alongside practical capability.

articles.title: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Data literacy in the labor market: a systematic review | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: High — systematic review methodology synthesises evidence across multiple studies and contexts, though generalisability depends on the quality and geographic diversity of included studies.
takeaways: Data literacy is increasingly critical for workforce competitiveness; identify which data skills (e.g., interpretation, visualisation, statistical reasoning) are most valued in your sector to target upskilling efforts.
Organisations can design targeted data literacy programmes by understanding which job roles and levels need foundational vs. advanced capabilities, rather than applying one-size-fits-all training.

Data literacy gaps persist across demographics and education levels in labour markets; audit your organisation's data skills baseline to identify underrepresented groups who may need additional support.

articles.title: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to higher vocational education context; generalisability to workplace AI literacy programs unclear without details on student demographics, institution types, and geographic scope.
takeaways: Consider adopting a competency-ladder framework (progressive skill levels) rather than one-size-fits-all AI training — this scaffolded approach may improve engagement and retention for learners with varying starting points.

Validate any AI literacy pathway you implement with your target audience before full rollout; the study emphasises the importance of testing competency frameworks to ensure they actually build capability in practice.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition — unclear from snippet alone whether findings apply broadly across sectors, geographies, and organisational contexts. The 'double-edged' framing suggests context-dependent effects that may vary by implementation approach.
takeaways: AI adoption can both enhance and inhibit employee creativity depending on implementation context — assess your organisation's current approach to determine whether AI is augmenting creative thinking or constraining it through over-automation or rigid workflows.

The mechanism linking AI adoption to creativity outcomes likely involves employee autonomy, skill development, and role clarity — design AI implementations that preserve creative decision-making space rather than replacing human judgment entirely.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings are specific to nursing contexts and medical AI implementation. Generalisability to other healthcare professions or non-healthcare sectors is unclear without knowing sample composition and geographic scope.
takeaways: When introducing medical AI systems, prioritise preserving or enhancing nurse autonomy in decision-making — the study suggests autonomy is the key mechanism linking AI readiness to improved wellbeing, not AI readiness alone.

Design AI implementations with nurses to maintain their clinical judgement and control over workflows; systems that reduce autonomy risk negating wellbeing benefits even if staff are technically ready for AI.

Monitor wellbeing outcomes longitudinally during AI rollout, not just adoption rates — three-wave data shows the relationship between readiness and wellbeing unfolds over time and is mediated by how much autonomy staff retain.

articles.title: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Competing strain and resource pathways linking AI-enabled work systems to employee wellbeing  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The competing strain-resource framework is conceptually robust but application to Australian workplaces would depend on sector, organisation size, and implementation context of AI systems.
takeaways: AI-enabled work systems create dual pathways affecting wellbeing — some aspects strain employees (e.g. monitoring, job uncertainty) while others provide resources (e.g. automation of routine tasks, decision support). Assess which pathways dominate in your context to target interventions.

Monitor both negative strain indicators (stress, autonomy loss) and positive resource indicators (skill development, efficiency gains) when implementing AI systems, rather than assuming net positive or negative impact on employee wellbeing.
Design AI implementations with attention to job redesign and upskilling opportunities to amplify resource pathways, and transparency/consultation practices to mitigate strain pathways.

articles.title: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Workers are facing an age of uncertainty  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Findings reflect US workforce dynamics and APA membership perspectives; may not fully generalise to Australian employment contexts, which have different regulatory frameworks, union structures, and labour market conditions.
takeaways: Acknowledge uncertainty as a psychological stressor affecting employee wellbeing and engagement — develop targeted mental health support and clear communication strategies to help staff navigate role ambiguity, particularly around AI integration.
Create structured forums for workers to voice concerns about job security and changing skill requirements; psychological safety depends on being heard, not just reassured.

Design transition support programs that address both practical reskilling and emotional responses to workplace change — uncertainty about AI's impact requires both capability development and psychological validation.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited by focus on paternalistic leadership contexts (common in East Asian organisations) and organisational psychological ownership as a specific mediating mechanism. Findings may not transfer readily to non-paternalistic or Western management contexts.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customisation and adaptation decisions — this sense of ownership directly increases collaboration with AI systems.
Under paternalistic leadership styles, employee-AI collaboration is strengthened when leaders frame AI as a shared organisational asset rather than a top-down imposition.

Enable 'AI crafting' practices (deliberate modification and personalisation of AI workflows) as a practical pathway to boost engagement with AI technologies, especially in hierarchical organisational cultures.

articles.title: Why AI Boosts Creativity for Some Employees but Not Others - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why AI Boosts Creativity for Some Employees but Not Others  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on expert commentary rather than empirical research. Findings likely reflect primarily Western, knowledge-worker perspectives and may not generalise across sectors, skill levels, or cultural contexts.
takeaways: Identify which employees view AI as a creative collaborator versus a threat to autonomy; those with higher psychological safety and growth mindset are more likely to benefit creatively from AI tools.

Create conditions for creative AI use by clarifying how AI augments rather than replaces human judgment, and provide training that emphasises exploration and experimentation rather than efficiency alone.
Monitor whether AI adoption widens or narrows creative output within teams — some employees may disengage if they perceive AI as diminishing their unique contribution or control over their work.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte report likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample characteristics, study design, and geographic scope are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Shift organisational change framing from 'AI adoption' (technical implementation) to 'AI adaptation' (behavioural transformation) — this reframing helps clarify that success depends on building new human capabilities and mindsets, not just deploying tools.
Design change interventions that explicitly target the behaviours and ways of working needed for AI use, rather than assuming employees will naturally adapt once technology is deployed.
Align people-focused change strategies with AI implementation timelines early, identifying capability gaps and resistance points before rollout to increase engagement and reduce adoption friction.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — full methodology needed to assess sample size, sectors included, and geographic scope. The theoretical focus on psychological capital and AI as a job resource may apply broadly to knowledge work, but sector and demographic limitations are unknown.
takeaways: Develop psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) in teams using AI tools — employees with stronger psychological capital are more likely to harness AI as a resource for innovation rather than resist it.

Frame AI systems as job resources during implementation: emphasize how they augment work and create opportunity, not just automate tasks. This mindset shift can unlock innovation potential in algorithm-driven roles.
Design onboarding and leadership communication to build confidence and agency around AI use — psychological capital is a malleable construct that can be strengthened through targeted interventions.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford-based perspective without specific empirical data on sample composition, geography, or sectors studied. Findings may reflect US higher education and tech-sector bias.
takeaways: Identify specific workplace tasks most vulnerable to AI automation in your organisation, then design targeted reskilling programs for affected staff before disruption occurs — this proactive stance builds psychological safety around change.

Frame AI adoption as a tool-augmentation conversation rather than a replacement threat; help employees understand how AI will reshape their role (not eliminate it), which reduces defensive behaviours and increases willingness to learn new capabilities.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's client work and industry observations, but specific case details and organisational contexts may vary. Applicability across different sectors and company sizes should be tested in your own context.
takeaways: Map your AI transformation across three phases (adoption, integration, impact) to clarify where your organisation currently sits and what capabilities or mindset shifts are needed to progress to the next horizon.

Design behaviour change strategies that evolve at each horizon — early adoption requires different change management levers (incentives, training) than later phases, which demand cultural embedding and redefined roles.

Identify and address the gap between AI adoption and measurable business impact by establishing clear success metrics and accountability before rolling out new AI tools, rather than assuming use automatically drives value.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — no geographic scope or sample characteristics disclosed in snippet. Appears to be a single-country study, likely China based on journal conventions, but cannot confirm from the title and snippet alone. Findings may not generalise broadly without knowing sector, organisational type, and workforce demographics.
takeaways: Employees' awareness of AI can trigger two distinct pathways to job crafting: through threat appraisal (stress-driven adaptation) and challenge appraisal (opportunity-driven redesign). Managers should diagnose which appraisal employees are experiencing to tailor support accordingly.

The Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework suggests that framing AI as a resource rather than a threat shifts employees toward proactive job crafting. Use transparent communication about AI's role and provide agency in how employees redesign their work.

Awareness of AI alone does not guarantee constructive job crafting—the cognitive pathway matters. Training should address both stress management (threat pathway) and opportunity recognition (challenge pathway) to enable adaptive behaviour change.

articles.title: Innovative technologies and workplace collaborations in the energy sector based in the United Arab Emirates - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Innovative technologies and workplace collaborations in the energy sector based in the United Arab Emirates  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings are specific to the UAE energy sector and may not generalise to other geographic regions or industries with different regulatory, cultural, or technological contexts.
takeaways: Identify which collaborative technologies are already embedded in your energy or similar high-stakes sector — audit existing adoption barriers (skill gaps, resistance to change, siloed workflows) before introducing new tools.

Design change initiatives that address sector-specific collaboration challenges rather than adopting generic technology rollouts — in energy, safety-critical operations and cross-functional teams may require tailored adoption strategies.
Engage frontline workers and technical staff early in technology selection to surface practical constraints and build buy-in, rather than top-down implementation.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — limited information provided about sample size, geographic scope, or methodological rigor. Neuroimaging findings often have modest effect sizes and may not translate uniformly across populations.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies consistently find structural or functional differences in individuals with psychopathic traits, particularly in regions associated with emotion processing and impulse control — a finding that's counterintuitive because it suggests observable neural correlates of psychological traits once thought purely behavioural.

The 'shocking difference' framing is typical of popular neuroscience reporting, but the actual biological basis of psychopathy remains complex and debated — brain differences don't explain why some people with similar neural profiles behave very differently.

This type of research fascinates because it sits at the intersection of nature versus nurture: if psychopathy has a neural signature, does that change how we think about moral responsibility and criminal justice?

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not detailed in the snippet; appears to be a controlled laboratory study of surprise and memory encoding, which may not fully capture how personality shapes memory for unexpected events in real-world contexts.
takeaways: People with different personality traits encode and remember surprising moments differently — your Big Five profile might predict whether you'll vividly recall an unexpected event or quickly move on.

The finding reveals why eyewitness accounts of the same surprise event can vary wildly between people; individual personality differences create genuinely different memory experiences, not just different reporting.

Curiosity about personality science: it's counterintuitive that surprise — something seemingly universal — would hit our brains so differently depending on who we are, yet the research suggests our traits fundamentally shape what sticks in memory.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — snippet provides minimal detail on study design, sample size, or geographic scope. A full article review would be needed to assess whether findings are preliminary observations or robust findings.
takeaways: A surprising biological link: an overactive thyroid may correlate with darker personality traits like narcissism or psychopathy — a counterintuitive connection between endocrine function and personality psychology.
Highlights how physical health conditions can have unexpected psychological dimensions, suggesting personality traits aren't purely psychological but may have measurable physiological correlates.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — synthesises research across multiple disciplines and populations, though primarily draws on Western psychology literature.
takeaways: Close friendships appear to have measurable protective effects on physical health—comparable in some studies to the impact of exercise or quitting smoking—making social connection a surprisingly powerful health intervention.

The relationship works both ways: people with strong friendships recover faster from illness and experience lower stress hormones, but lonely people show accelerated aging at the cellular level, suggesting isolation is genuinely taxing on the body.

Counterintuitively, it's the quality of friendships that matters far more than quantity; one or two deeply supportive relationships confer more health benefit than a large network of casual acquaintances.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — findings suggest music-personality links are consistent across diverse cultures and geographic regions.
takeaways: People with similar personalities tend to like similar music regardless of where they live — suggesting something universal about how personality shapes musical taste.
Your music playlist might actually be a pretty reliable window into your personality traits, which is a fun way to think about why your colleague's taste seems so 'them'.
This challenges the idea that musical preference is purely cultural; there's a deeper personality-driven logic to why we're drawn to certain sounds.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesizes psychological research on true crime consumption, but scope and specific studies reviewed are unclear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: People's obsession with true crime isn't morbid curiosity gone wrong—it likely taps into deep psychological needs like understanding danger, solving puzzles, and feeling safer by learning how crimes happen.
True crime fascinates across demographics in ways that challenge the stereotype of who gets hooked; psychological perspectives reveal universal human drives rather than personality defects.

The appeal reveals something interesting about how our brains balance fear and control—we voluntarily expose ourselves to dark stories from a safe distance, which may actually satisfy our need to process risk.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad global perspective, though representativeness depends on PwC's sampling methodology and respondent demographics (typically skews towards larger organisations and developed economies). Findings reflect 2026 snapshot and may not capture smaller organisations or informal sectors.
takeaways: Identify specific workforce anxieties and hopes from the 2026 data to tailor psychological safety interventions — safety messaging resonates better when it addresses documented employee concerns rather than assumed ones.
Use survey findings to benchmark your organisation's psychological safety climate against global patterns and peer expectations, helping prioritise where to focus culture-building efforts.

Where the survey reveals gaps between hopes and fears, these represent high-leverage areas for leadership communication and trust-building — transparency about organisational response to these concerns strengthens psychological safety.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The conceptual model (AI adoption → psychological safety → depression) may apply across sectors, but geographic scope and sample size are unclear.
takeaways: AI adoption can undermine psychological safety if not accompanied by ethical leadership; monitor employee wellbeing (depression indicators) when rolling out AI initiatives, and pair adoption with explicit ethical frameworks and transparent communication.

Leaders must actively foster psychological safety during AI transitions—create spaces where employees can voice concerns about AI impacts without fear, and ensure ethical leadership practices are visible and consistent throughout the change process.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone. Full article review needed to determine sample size, geographic scope, sector coverage, and whether findings apply beyond algorithm-driven roles.
takeaways: Psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) may be a key lever for fostering innovation when AI tools are introduced — consider assessing and developing these capacities in teams transitioning to AI-augmented work.

AI adoption threatens psychological safety when employees fear displacement or loss of autonomy; proactively building confidence in one's ability to work alongside AI systems could mitigate anxiety and unlock the resource potential of AI tools.

Organisations should monitor whether AI is being experienced as a job resource (enhancing capability) or a threat to psychological safety — the gap between these perceptions may explain why some teams innovate with AI while others disengage.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG practitioner report based on consulting experience, but lacks transparent methodology, sample size details, or geographic specificity. Findings likely drawn from client engagements across multiple sectors and geographies, but generalisability depends on undisclosed sample composition.
takeaways: Psychological safety reduces status-based hierarchies and power imbalances, enabling quieter or marginalised employees to contribute ideas — consider how your team's speaking patterns correlate with formal role or seniority, and design interventions (e.g., anonymous input channels, structured turn-taking) to equalise voice.

When psychological safety is present, employees from underrepresented groups report higher engagement and belonging — audit whether your onboarding, meeting norms, and feedback practices inadvertently silence certain demographics, and measure inclusion outcomes alongside psychological safety scores.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings — while psychological safety is universally relevant, this report reflects American workplace contexts, labour market conditions, and workforce demographics that may differ from Australian settings.
takeaways: Identify which specific workplace conditions (e.g., blame culture, unclear expectations, leadership micromanagement) are eroding psychological safety in your team, then pilot targeted interventions to rebuild trust and candour.

Use data from this APA report to make the business case for psychological safety investment to leadership — frame it in terms of retention, engagement, and error reporting (key concerns in the 2024 US context).
Audit whether your current onboarding, feedback, and escalation processes actually invite employees to speak up about mistakes or concerns, or if they inadvertently punish vulnerability.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global client work and surveys, but findings may reflect practices in large, well-resourced organisations and may not generalise to smaller firms or resource-constrained settings.
takeaways: Frame AI capability-building as 'superagency'—enabling employees to act with greater autonomy and impact—rather than automation or replacement; this framing supports psychological safety by positioning AI as augmenting human agency.

Design AI adoption programmes that explicitly address fears of job displacement and skill obsolescence; psychological safety requires transparent communication about how roles will evolve and what new capabilities employees are expected to develop.

Create structured opportunities for hands-on AI experimentation in low-stakes environments; employees who feel safe to explore, make mistakes, and learn with AI are more likely to unlock its full potential in their roles.
